issues.description: The abstract, title, and analysis repeatedly frame the outcome as 'willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment' and 'willingness to make sacrifices for the environment,' yet the Measures section states environmentalism was operationalized as 'concern about environmental problems' using two items measuring concern and perceived exaggeration. Concern and willingness to sacrifice are distinct constructs; the central dependent variable is mislabeled throughout, undermining interpretation of all results.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, “How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?” and “To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?”.

issues.description: The sample is described in the Methods as recruited 'through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington,' clearly a student sample. Yet the abstract, introduction, and discussion repeatedly describe it as a 'national probability sample' and 'nationally representative sample,' and the entire interpretive framework hinges on contrasting this 'general population sample' with prior student samples. This is a fundamental contradiction that invalidates the central inferential claims.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington.

issues.description: The claim that results are 'highly generalisable' to the New Zealand population is unsupported. The sample is 374 introductory psychology students with mean age 19, 68% female, 86% Pākehā—not nationally representative on age, education, or gender. Calling this 'nationally representative' is a serious generalizability overclaim contradicted by the reported demographics.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: The study claims to span five years (2009-2013) across five time points but states data come from 'five semesters,' and the introductory-pool recruitment implies a semester-based interval. Five semesters do not equal five years, and the sampling interval is unclear. This affects the entire 'five-year cross-lagged' framing.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).

issues.description: Despite explicitly acknowledging early in the paper that 'it is therefore inappropriate to draw comments on the direction of any temporal association,' the discussion repeatedly makes strong causal claims (e.g., SDO 'having a causal effect,' 'the desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism'). Cross-lagged panel models cannot establish causation, especially with unmeasured confounds, and the authors even note a third-variable explanation is plausible, contradicting their causal language.
issues.quote: With our findings of a temporal connection between SDO and environmentalism, this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes, and perhaps even being foundational for these attitudes.

issues.description: Throughout the results, regression coefficients are reported with 'SD' (e.g., 'B = -.11, SD = .01'). These are almost certainly standard errors, not standard deviations. Mislabeling standard errors as standard deviations is a statistical reporting error that misleads readers about precision and is inconsistent with the accompanying confidence intervals.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.description: For the SDO-on-RWA path, the coefficient is reported as B = .02 with a 95% CI of [.02, .03], yet the reverse RWA-on-SDO is also B = .02. More problematically, the reported lagged effect of RWA on SDO (B = .02) and SDO on RWA (B = -.001) are described, but the Wald test comparing them yields χ²(1) = 15,389.13—an implausibly enormous value for comparing two small, similar-magnitude paths, suggesting an error in the reported statistic or constraints.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001), a finding we explore more fully in the Discussion.

issues.description: The analysis used listwise deletion across five waves of longitudinal data, which typically produces substantial attrition and biased estimates if dropout is non-random. No attrition analysis, retention rates, or comparison of completers vs. dropouts is provided, and the authors defer all sample/retention details to a website. FIML or multiple imputation would be standard; listwise deletion is inappropriate here.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: Critical information about the sample, procedure, retention, and demographics is deferred entirely to an external website rather than reported in the manuscript, preventing readers from evaluating attrition, missingness, measurement timing, and representativeness. This undermines replicability and evaluation.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: The acknowledgments and references attribute the data to the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study (NZAVS), a national longitudinal study, while the Methods state recruitment was through a university introductory psychology pool. These two descriptions of the data source are mutually inconsistent and cannot both be true; the discrepancy must be resolved as it determines whether the central student-vs-general-population argument holds.
issues.quote: We express our gratitude to the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study (NZAVS) team for their work collecting and maintaining the NZAVS.

issues.description: Reliabilities are described as 'poorer than is typically the case' but no actual reliability coefficients (e.g., Cronbach's alpha or omega) are reported for the scales. The diagonal values in Table 1 (.69, .70, .76) may be reliabilities, but this is not stated. Low reliability attenuates observed relationships and complicates comparison of predictor strength (SDO vs. RWA), yet this is not addressed.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31].

issues.description: One RWA item was not assessed at Time 2 but included at all other time points. This creates non-equivalent measurement across waves for a model that imposes time-invariant constraints (including equal residual variances per item), potentially biasing parameter estimates. The handling of this missing item in the constrained model is not explained.
issues.quote: The item “Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done”, was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: The authors conclude SDO is a 'statistically stronger predictor' than RWA, but their own constrained-model comparison (χ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126) indicates NO significant difference between the SDO and RWA paths to environmentalism. They nonetheless interpret SDO as stronger 'based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients,' which directly contradicts their non-significant test and overstates the difference.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.description: The Methods state a significance threshold of p < .05, while Figure 1's caption states all paths 'meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01.' These conflicting thresholds create ambiguity about which criterion was applied and raise concerns about analytic flexibility in threshold selection.
issues.quote: All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.description: CFI = .86 is below conventional acceptable thresholds (~.90-.95), indicating poor fit. The authors dismiss this as due to 'model complexity' and accept the model based on RMSEA and SRMR, but CFI is not primarily a complexity-driven index in the way claimed (it is sensitive to model misspecification). Accepting a model with CFI = .86 without further justification or re-specification is questionable.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: No pre-registration is mentioned despite directional hypotheses being stated. The model involves numerous researcher degrees of freedom (which paths to constrain, residual variance equality constraints, stationarity assumptions, item selection). The choice to impose time-invariance was justified post hoc by analytic interest, and the alternative to the Wald test was constructed ad hoc, raising concerns about undisclosed flexibility.
issues.quote: Due to the nature of the analysis and the constraints placed on the model, the traditional Wald test to confirm that SDO is a statistically stronger predictor than RWA is not possible. Instead, we imposed similar constraints on the model as in the Wald test

issues.description: The finding that RWA predicts SDO but not vice versa is interpreted as evidence that 'New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.' This is a substantial theoretical leap from a single asymmetric cross-lagged coefficient (which may reflect differential reliability, variance, or measurement properties rather than socialization processes), and constitutes overinterpretation.
issues.quote: Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.

issues.description: SDO and RWA were each measured with only six items, and environmentalism with only two items, from longer validated scales. Such drastic abbreviation (especially a 2-item DV) reduces content validity and reliability, and no justification, validation, or factor structure verification of the short forms is provided beyond a citation, weakening construct measurement.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale

issues.description: No time-invariant or time-varying covariates (age, gender, political party, income, education) are included in the model, despite these being plausible common causes of both ideology and environmentalism. Traditional cross-lagged panel models without accounting for stable trait-level confounds (e.g., via random-intercept CLPM) are known to conflate between-person and within-person effects, biasing causal-directional inferences.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.subcategory: missing item-level and full correlation reporting
issues.description: Only Time 1 descriptives and correlations are reported (Table 1). Correlations and descriptives across the other four waves, the full matrix needed to evaluate the cross-lagged model, and the actual stability coefficients (only described qualitatively as 'stable') are not reported in numeric form, impeding evaluation and replication.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1.

issues.description: The title references 'environmentalism' broadly, the abstract references 'willingness to change behaviour,' but the measured construct is environmental concern (attitudinal, not behavioral). The slippage between behavioral willingness, sacrifice, and concern across title, abstract, and methods constitutes a construct operationalization mismatch that affects how findings should be interpreted and generalized.
issues.quote: We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment in a national probability sample over five years.

issues.description: The Methods state 'We present standardized parameters,' but Figure 1 is captioned as 'Unstandardized parameters' and the results report unstandardized B coefficients. This inconsistency about whether standardized or unstandardized estimates are presented affects interpretation, particularly the cross-construct comparison of predictor strength, where standardization matters.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances.

issues.subcategory: misattributed comparison to prior longitudinal study
issues.description: The paper attributes the reversal of findings (SDO stronger here vs. RWA stronger in Stanley et al. [14]) entirely to sample type (general vs. student). However, the present sample is itself a student sample per the Methods, undermining this central explanatory account. The interpretation rests on an unverified sample-type contrast that is contradicted by the manuscript's own recruitment description.
issues.quote: It is likely that the difference in sample type therefore accounts for the differences in our results, as we used a general population sample.

issues.description: Throughout the results the chi-square test statistic is rendered as '2(1)' rather than 'χ²(1)', and degrees of freedom and exact values are inconsistently formatted. While likely a typographic issue, the unclear notation (e.g., what test '2(1) = 2.34' refers to) reduces clarity needed to verify the model comparisons.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126

issues.description: The findings on SDO-RWA associations are explicitly tied to New Zealand's 'highly polarized' political system, yet the broad conclusions about ideology and environmentalism are generalized without adequately limiting them to this context. The cross-national variability in SDO-RWA relations the authors themselves cite implies limited generalizability that is under-acknowledged.
issues.quote: Duckitt [3] shows relatively strong associations between SDO and RWA cross-sectionally in New Zealand, while in other contexts the relationship tends to be weaker or non-significant.
